prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, taking the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a new measurement technique in the strict sense: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors while interrogating very many atoms at once, and Ye's group then drove accuracy and stability to about 1e-18. Five of the six members who ranked it placed it in their top three, and independent laboratories (RIKEN, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and others) have reproduced and compared such clocks, including over fibre links, so the result has been through the calibration and systematics test that I use as my own yardstick. It enables tests of fundamental constants, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and relativistic geodesy, and prepares the redefinition of the second. The credit is compact: a two-person configuration with a clear inventor and a clear leader of the precision frontier. After listening to colleagues I move it ahead of my own opening first choice, B023, because it combines strong scientific merit with broad committee support that I can defend.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and adjacency. The 2005 prize (Hall, Hansch) gave the frequency comb on which Ye's work leans, and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) covered the control of single quantum systems and ion clocks, so a sceptic can call lattice clocks a refinement of recognised ground. Lemonde, Takamoto and others also made important contributions to the lattice-clock realisation, and the formal redefinition of the second has not yet happened. There is also a risk that metrology is judged by its applications, which are still developing, rather than by a discovery about nature.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B008) first as a new classification of electronic states, with Kane and Mele supplying the decisive theory and Molenkamp the first experiment, and he places the optical lattice clocks only sixth.
responses.response: I agree that B008 is a conceptual advance and I do not downgrade it: it is my first alternative and I would not oppose it. I am not convinced it should win outright, because the credit problem is real. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe effect that Molenkamp then measured, and Zhang cannot be rewarded now. A prize that credits a measured result to Molenkamp while leaving out the proposal he tested is the kind of attribution we should avoid. Lattice clocks have a cleaner chain from proposal to demonstration to precision frontier. I also lean on you and Mehlig for the condensed-matter weighting, which is outside my expertise.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube (B023) first: a cubic-kilometre detector in ice opened neutrino astronomy, and the instrument concept matters as much as the diffuse flux, with Halzen, Karle and Spiering a fair trio.
responses.response: I ranked B023 first myself, so I share the instrument argument, and I think you are right that the flux is confirmed in several channels. But only five members ranked it and Johansson placed it seventh. The credit also worries me more than we said in our openings: the AMANDA and DUMAND founders, and a collaboration of hundreds, sit behind three names, and I could not say with confidence which three designed the decisive features. I therefore keep B023 as a live alternative and would be glad to see it go forward when the attribution is clearer and the source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) are firmer.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first, crediting Katori with the clean invention and Ye with the leading realisation, and sees the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as acknowledged but not blocking.
responses.response: We largely agree, and I find your two-name attribution convincing. I would put the overlap question more carefully than your opening does. The comb prize rewarded a tool for counting optical cycles, and the ion-clock work rewarded control of single quantum systems; neither covers the many-atom, Lamb-Dicke, magic-wavelength approach that gives the stability. I would write the citation around that idea so the prize does not look like a repeat. Where I stay cautious is the contribution from strontium and ytterbium groups outside these two names, which we cannot settle from the list.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B004) first as the architecture behind current superconducting processors, distinct from the 2025 prize, and himself flags close professional ties to that community and a possible recusal.
responses.response: I accept that circuit QED is distinct in content from the 2025 macroscopic-tunnelling work, but I do not think timing helps it: coming one year after a circuit prize, it would look repetitive to outsiders, and Kroll and Eriksson raised the same concern. The attribution gap is serious too, since Girvin is outside the three credited names, and Yale's role in the architecture would be hard to describe fairly. Your own recusal flag matters; as Chair I would suggest you decide whether to step out of the B004 discussion, and I would value your view on lattice clocks in atomic physics.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first as a new way of measuring time, and also ranks squeezed light (B012) second as a quantum resource that improves the most precise instruments.
responses.response: I share the measurement-first view on B035. On B012, you are right that the gain in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 is observed and concrete, which is why it was in my top six. But the credit is spread over Caves, Kimble, Slusher, Walls, Mavalvala, Schnabel and McKenzie, and no three people describe it fairly. LIGO already received a prize in 2017 for the detection, so I do not rank squeezing above clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, or other lattice-clock groups have a claim strong enough to challenge a two-person configuration.
Whether the B008 attribution (BHZ proposal for HgTe) can be resolved well enough for the colleagues who ranked it first to support it as a prize.
I cannot independently verify the early AMANDA and IceCube design history needed for B023 attribution.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B035 or B008 from my profile. My own collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur) are in astroparticle physics, which is adjacent to IceCube (B023); my profile lists no named link to Halzen, Karle or Spiering, but the committee may want to note the field closeness if B023 is advanced.
